topics.title: P & NP Classes
topics.keyConcept: Class P contains problems solvable in polynomial time deterministically. Class NP contains problems whose solutions are verifiable in polynomial time deterministically.
topics.content:
Complexity theory classifies computational problems based on the resources (time and space) required to solve them. We focus on **decision problems** (problems with a Yes/No answer):

  • Class P (Polynomial Time): The class of decision problems that can be solved by a deterministic Turing machine (our standard computers) in polynomial time \( O(n^k) \) for some constant \( k \). These are considered 'tractable' or easily solvable problems. Examples: searching (linear/binary), sorting (mergesort/heapsort), and shortest path (Dijkstra).
  • Class NP (Nondeterministic Polynomial Time): The class of decision problems where a candidate solution can be verified by a deterministic Turing machine in polynomial time. That is, if someone gives you a 'certificate' (candidate solution), you can check if it is correct in polynomial time. If a problem is in P, it is also in NP (meaning \( P \subseteq NP \)).

Real-World Project Example: Finding the shortest route between two cities on a map is in Class P (Dijkstra's algorithm solves it). However, finding a Sudoku solution is in Class NP: finding the solution is hard, but verifying a completed grid simply requires checking that numbers 1-9 do not duplicate, which is easy (polynomial time).
topics.commonMistakes: Stating that 'NP' stands for 'Non-Polynomial'. This is incorrect. NP stands for Nondeterministic Polynomial time, representing problems solvable in polynomial time by a theoretical Nondeterministic Turing machine.
topics.interviewTip: The P vs. NP question is one of the most famous unsolved problems in computer science. If asked, explain that 'P' represents problems that are easy to *solve*, while 'NP' represents problems that are easy to *verify* (once you are given a candidate solution).

topics.title: NP-Hard & NP-Complete Classes
topics.keyConcept: NP-Hard problems are at least as hard as any problem in NP. NP-Complete problems are the hardest problems in NP, representing the intersection of NP and NP-Hard.
topics.content:
To classify the hardest problems in NP, we use **Polynomial-Time Reduction**: if we can transform problem A into problem B in polynomial time, then solving B solves A. This means B is at least as hard as A. Based on this, we define:

  • NP-Hard: A problem \( X \) is NP-hard if any problem \( Y \in NP \) can be reduced to \( X \) in polynomial time. NP-hard problems do not have to be in NP themselves (and do not have to be decision problems).
  • NP-Complete: A problem \( X \) is NP-complete if: (1) \( X \in NP \), and (2) \( X \) is NP-hard. They represent the absolute hardest problems in NP. If any single NP-complete problem can be solved in polynomial time (i.e. is found to be in P), then \( P = NP \).

Real-World Project Example: The **Traveling Salesperson Decision Problem** (TSP: is there a tour of length at most $K$?) is NP-complete. An optimization version of TSP (find the absolute shortest path) is NP-hard, because it is not a simple Yes/No decision problem and cannot belong to NP directly.
topics.commonMistakes: Thinking that all NP-hard problems are NP-complete. An NP-complete problem must belong to Class NP (be verifiable in polynomial time). An NP-hard problem like the Halting Problem is undecidable and does not belong to NP.
topics.interviewTip: If an interviewer asks: 'How do you prove a new problem is NP-complete?', outline a two-step proof: (1) prove the problem belongs to Class NP, and (2) pick an existing NP-complete problem (like 3-SAT) and show a polynomial-time reduction from it to the new problem.

topics.title: Cook's Theorem & Classic NP-Complete Problems
topics.keyConcept: Cook's Theorem proved that the Boolean Satisfiability (SAT) problem is NP-complete. Other NPC problems are proven by reducing SAT to them.
topics.content:
Cook's Theorem (Cook-Levin Theorem): Proved that the Boolean Satisfiability Problem (SAT) is NP-complete. This was the first problem shown to be NP-complete. The proof established that any decision problem solvable by a nondeterministic Turing machine in polynomial time can be reduced to a boolean formula that is satisfiable if and only if the machine accepts the input. This allowed researchers to prove hundreds of other problems are NP-complete via reduction, creating the NPC family.

Classic NP-complete problems include:

  • 3-SAT: SAT restricted to clauses with exactly 3 literals.
  • Hamiltonian Cycle: Finding a cycle in a graph that visits every vertex exactly once.
  • Vertex Cover: Finding a subset of vertices of size $k$ that touches every edge in the graph.
  • Clique: Finding a subset of $k$ vertices in a graph that are all pairwise adjacent (complete subgraph).
  • Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP): Finding a tour of vertices with total weight $\le K$.

Real-World Project Example: Resource scheduling. A university scheduling system assigning exams to slots under constraints (no teacher double-booked, no student has two exams at once) is a graph coloring problem, which is a classic NP-complete problem.
topics.commonMistakes: Confusing a Hamiltonian Cycle with an Eulerian Cycle. A Hamiltonian cycle visits every vertex once (NP-complete). An Eulerian cycle visits every edge once and can be solved in linear time \( O(V+E) \) (belongs to Class P).

topics.title: Approximation Algorithms
topics.keyConcept: Approximation algorithms solve NP-hard optimization problems in polynomial time, guaranteeing solutions within a bounding ratio of the absolute optimum.
topics.content:
Since we cannot solve NP-complete problems optimally in polynomial time (unless \( P = NP \)), we use **Approximation Algorithms**. These are polynomial-time algorithms that find a solution close to the optimal solution. An approximation algorithm has an **approximation ratio \( ho(n) \)** if for any input of size \( n \), the cost \( C \) of the solution satisfies: \[ \frac{1}{\rho(n)} \le \frac{C}{C^*} \le \rho(n) \] where \( C^* \) is the optimal cost. If a minimization algorithm has a ratio of 2, the returned path cost is at most twice the optimal path cost.

Worked Example (Vertex Cover): A simple 2-approximation algorithm for Vertex Cover works as follows:

function approxVertexCover(Graph G):
    C = {} // Initialize empty cover set
    E' = G.edges // Copy of edges
    while E' is not empty:
        Let (u, v) be an arbitrary edge in E'
        Add u and v to C
        Remove from E' all edges incident to u or v
    return C

This algorithm runs in polynomial time \( O(V + E) \) and guarantees that the size of the vertex cover \( |C| \le 2 \times |C^*| \) (at most double the size of the optimal cover).
topics.commonMistakes: Thinking that approximation algorithms are heuristics with no mathematical bounds. Heuristics (like genetic algorithms or simulated annealing) have no guarantee of how close they get to the optimum; approximation algorithms have a mathematically proven bounding ratio.

practiceQuestions.question: What is the difference between Class P and Class NP?
practiceQuestions.answer: Class P consists of decision problems that can be solved in polynomial time by a deterministic Turing machine (e.g., finding a shortest path). Class NP consists of decision problems where a proposed solution can be verified in polynomial time by a deterministic Turing machine, even though finding the solution might take exponential time (e.g., Sudoku or Subset Sum).

practiceQuestions.question: Define NP-Complete and NP-Hard. How do they relate to each other?
practiceQuestions.answer: A problem is NP-Hard if every problem in NP can be reduced to it in polynomial time. A problem is NP-Complete if it is both in NP and is NP-Hard. Therefore, NP-Complete is the intersection of Class NP and NP-Hard. NP-Complete represents the hardest decision problems in NP.

practiceQuestions.question: State the significance of Cook's Theorem.
practiceQuestions.answer: Cook's Theorem proved that the Boolean Satisfiability Problem (SAT) is NP-complete. It was the first problem proven to be NP-complete. Its significance lies in the fact that it allows researchers to prove other problems are NP-complete simply by reducing SAT to them in polynomial time, rather than proving it from first principles.

practiceQuestions.question: What is a polynomial-time reduction? How is it used to prove NP-completeness?
practiceQuestions.answer: A polynomial-time reduction is a method of transforming problem A into problem B in polynomial time. To prove problem B is NP-complete: (1) we prove B is in NP, and (2) we select a known NP-complete problem A (like SAT or Vertex Cover) and show that A can be reduced to B in polynomial time. This implies that if we could solve B easily, we could also solve A easily.

practiceQuestions.question: What is an approximation algorithm? Define its approximation ratio.
practiceQuestions.answer: An approximation algorithm is a polynomial-time algorithm used to find near-optimal solutions to NP-hard optimization problems. Its performance is measured by its approximation ratio \( \rho(n) \), which bounds the ratio of the algorithm's solution cost to the absolute optimal solution cost.

mcqs.question: What does 'NP' stand for in complexity theory?
mcqs.explanation: NP stands for Nondeterministic Polynomial time, representing problems solvable in polynomial time by a nondeterministic Turing machine.

mcqs.question: If a problem is in Class P, then which of the following is also true?
options: It is NP-hard but not in NP
mcqs.explanation: Because any problem solvable in deterministic polynomial time is also verifiable in polynomial time, Class P is a subset of Class NP (\(P \subseteq NP\)).

mcqs.question: Which theorem proved that the Boolean Satisfiability Problem (SAT) is NP-complete?
mcqs.explanation: Cook's Theorem (or the Cook-Levin Theorem) established that SAT is NP-complete, marking the birth of NP-completeness theory.

mcqs.question: A problem X is NP-complete if:
options: X is in P and NP-hard
X is in NP and is NP-hard
X is NP-hard and cannot be verified
X can be solved in linear time
mcqs.explanation: By definition, a problem is NP-complete if it is in NP (verifiable in polynomial time) and is NP-hard (all NP problems reduce to it).

mcqs.question: Which of the following problems is NOT NP-complete?
mcqs.explanation: Dijkstra's single-source shortest path is in P because it can be solved in polynomial time \(O(E \log V)\).

mcqs.question: If an approximation algorithm for a minimization problem has an approximation ratio of 2, what does this mean?
options: The solution cost will be at most half of the optimal cost
The solution cost will be at most double the optimal cost
The algorithm takes twice as long to run
The algorithm uses twice as much memory
mcqs.explanation: For minimization, an approximation ratio of 2 (or a 2-approximation) guarantees the returned solution cost is at most 2 times the absolute minimum cost.

mcqs.question: A deterministic Turing machine is equivalent to which of the following?
options: A standard physical computer executing sequential instructions
A quantum computer executing infinite states
A system that runs without power
mcqs.explanation: A deterministic Turing machine models standard sequential computation where each state transition is uniquely determined.

mcqs.question: What is the relationship between NP-hard and NP-complete problems?
options: NP-hard is a subset of P
mcqs.explanation: All NP-complete problems are NP-hard by definition. NP-complete is the subset of NP-hard problems that also belong to NP.

mcqs.question: Reducing problem A to problem B in polynomial time implies:
options: A is harder than or equal to B
B is harder than or equal to A
They are both solvable in O(1) time
mcqs.explanation: Reducing A to B means we can use B's solver to solve A. Thus, B is at least as hard as A.

mcqs.question: The Hamiltonian Path problem asks if a graph contains a path that:
options: Connects all vertices with minimum edge weights
mcqs.explanation: A Hamiltonian Path visits every vertex in the graph exactly once. (Visiting every edge exactly once is an Eulerian Path).
